2	title: Transcript Compaction

4	author: "soph"

9	
10	## TL;DR
11	
12	Session transcripts on `entire/checkpoints/v1` are 96.5% larger than what the UI needs. We introduce:
13	
14	1. **Dual-write:** CLI writes both raw transcript (`full.jsonl`) and compact **Entire Transcript Format** (`transcript.jsonl`) at condensation time.
15	2. **Split storage:** Permanent data (metadata + compact transcripts) goes on an append-only `/main` ref. Raw logs go on a separate `/full/current` ref that rotates into numbered archived generations when full. All stored under `refs/entire/` — invisible in GitHub's branch UI.
16	3. **Cleanup = delete entire generations.** No tree surgery, no force-push, no history rewriting. Just delete the archived ref — all blobs become unreachable.
17	
18	Only 2-3 active refs at any time. The CLI stays append-only. The API reads only the compact format.
19	
20	## Problem
21	
22	Session transcripts stored on `entire/checkpoints/v1` are significantly larger than what the UI needs. Claude Code's JSONL format includes streaming progress, subagent messages, thinking blocks, full tool output, and per-message metadata that the API parser never reads.
23	
24	Across 10 real transcripts (158 MB total), **96.5% of the data is unnecessary for the UI**. Individual files ranged from 63% to 99.9% reduction. Heavy subagent sessions (common with Task tool usage) can be 46 MB raw but only 40 KB after stripping.
25	
26	Additionally, transcripts grow over a session — when a user makes multiple commits, each checkpoint stores the full transcript up to that point. The second checkpoint contains everything from the first plus new lines. This duplication is intentional: `entire resume` needs the complete transcript to reconstruct conversation state, and storing the full log at each checkpoint means resume works from any single checkpoint without concatenating prior ones. But after the resume window passes, this duplication is pure waste.
27	
28	## Proposed Solution
29	
30	### Dual-write: raw + compact format
31	
32	Rather than only storing agent-native transcripts and stripping them later, the CLI writes **two files** to **two separate refs** at condensation time:
33	
34	1. **`full.jsonl`** → written to the ephemeral `/full/current` ref. Raw agent transcript (unchanged). Used by `entire resume` to reconstruct conversation state. Deleted with its generation after the retention window.
35	2. **`transcript.jsonl`** → written to the permanent `/main` ref. Compact **Entire Transcript Format**. Agent-agnostic, contains only what the UI/API needs. Never deleted.
36	
37	This addresses several concerns from the original RFD review:
38	
39	- **Rome (API) only needs to understand one format** — not Claude, Cursor, Gemini, Codex, and Copilot transcripts individually (Georg's point). Agent-specific parsing stays in the CLI; the API reads only the Entire Transcript Format.
40	- **No risky post-hoc transformation** — the compact format is written at recording time by the same CLI version that understands the agent's format. No version skew between writer and compactor.
41	- **Cleanup becomes simple deletion** — raw logs live in separate, ephemeral refs. After the retention window, delete the entire ref — no tree surgery, no force-push.
42	
43	### Entire Transcript Format
44	
45	A normalized, agent-agnostic JSONL format. One line per conversational turn. Versioned so the API can handle format evolution.
46	
47	The first line is a **header** declaring the format version and the source agent:
48	
49	```jsonl
50	{"v":1,"agent":"claude-code","cli_version":"0.42.0"}
51	```
52	
53	Subsequent lines are conversational entries:
54	
55	```jsonl
56	{"v":1,"type":"user","ts":"...","content":"user message text"}
57	{"v":1,"type":"user_tool_result","ts":"...","tool_use_id":"toolu_xxx","result":{"type":"text","file":"path"}}
58	{"v":1,"type":"assistant","ts":"...","id":"msg_xxx","content":[{"type":"text","text":"..."},{"type":"tool_use","id":"toolu_xxx","name":"Read","input":{...}}]}
59	```
60	
61	Every line carries `"v":1` so readers can handle format evolution without needing to read the header first (e.g., when streaming or reading from an offset). When we add or change fields, we bump the version. Old readers ignore unknown versions; new readers handle both.
62	
63	**Entry types:**
64	- `user` — user text messages: `type`, `ts`, `content`
65	- `user_tool_result` — tool results: `type`, `ts`, `tool_use_id`, result metadata (`type`, `file`, `error`, `answers`)
66	- `assistant` — assistant responses: `type`, `ts`, `id`, `content` (text + tool_use blocks only; thinking blocks dropped)
67	
68	**What's excluded (compared to raw agent transcripts):**
69	- All `progress`/`system`/`file-history-snapshot`/`queue-operation` entries
70	- Envelope fields (`parentUuid`, `cwd`, `sessionId`, `version`, `gitBranch`, etc.)
71	- Thinking blocks + signatures
72	- `message.usage` (already aggregated in `metadata.json`)
73	- Tool result content text (only linkage metadata kept)
74	- `progress:agent_progress` (subagent streaming)
75	- Binary data (externalized — see below)
76	
77	### Binary asset externalization
78	
79	Binary data in transcripts (user-provided images, screenshots) is extracted from the raw transcript and stored in the permanent `/main` ref alongside the compact transcript:
80	
81	```
82	refs/entire/checkpoints/v2/main → tree:
83	  <id[:2]>/<id[2:]>/
84	  ├── metadata.json
85	  ├── 0/
86	  │   ├── metadata.json
87	  │   ├── transcript.jsonl        # Compact Entire Transcript Format
88	  │   ├── transcript_hash.txt     # SHA-256 of transcript.jsonl
89	  │   ├── prompt.txt
90	  │   └── assets/                 # Externalized binary data
91	  │       ├── img-001.png
92	  │       └── img-002.jpg
93	  └── 1/
94	      └── ...
95	
96	refs/entire/checkpoints/v2/full/current → tree:
97	  <id[:2]>/<id[2:]>/
98	  ├── 0/
99	  │   ├── full.jsonl              # Raw agent transcript
100	  │   └── content_hash.txt        # SHA-256 of full.jsonl
101	  └── 1/
102	      └── ...
103	```
104	
105	The compact transcript references assets by relative path (e.g., `{"type":"image","path":"assets/img-001.png"}`).
106	
107	The raw transcript in `/full/current` still contains the inline base64-encoded images — that's the unmodified agent output. But since `/full/*` refs are ephemeral and get deleted as generations, the binary data survives in `/main` via the externalized `assets/` folder.
108	
109	### Content hash placement
110	
111	Each transcript format has its own SHA-256 hash file, co-located with the data it validates:
112	
113	- **`content_hash.txt`** on `/full/*` — hash of `full.jsonl` (raw transcript)
114	- **`transcript_hash.txt`** on `/main` — hash of `transcript.jsonl` (compact transcript)
115	
116	Both use the same format: `sha256:<hex-digest>`.
117	
118	#### Why `content_hash.txt` lives on `/full/*`
119	
120	`content_hash.txt` is a hash of `full.jsonl` and lives on `/full/*` alongside it, not on `/main`. This is deliberate:

120	`content_hash.txt` is a hash of `full.jsonl` and lives on `/full/*` alongside it, not on `/main`. This is deliberate:
121	
122	- **It validates ephemeral data.** The hash is computed from `full.jsonl` — a file that normally only exists on `/full/*` refs unless pinned to `/main`. Storing the hash on `/main` would leave a dangling reference to data that gets deleted with its generation.
123	- **It shares the same lifecycle.** When a generation is deleted, both the raw transcript and its integrity hash disappear together. No orphaned validation artifacts accumulate on the permanent ref.
124	- **`/main` doesn't need it.** The API reads `transcript.jsonl` (the compact format) from `/main` and does not consume `content_hash.txt`. Tests that validate transcript integrity operate against `full.jsonl` on `/full/*`, where both the data and its hash are co-located.
125	- **Pinning preserves the pair.** When a checkpoint is pinned, both `full.jsonl` and `content_hash.txt` are copied to `/main` together — the hash remains valid and useful for integrity checks on the pinned data.
126	
127	#### Why `transcript_hash.txt` lives on `/main`
128	
129	`transcript_hash.txt` is a hash of `transcript.jsonl` and lives on `/main` alongside it. This enables integrity validation of the compact transcript — the permanent, API-facing format — without depending on ephemeral `/full/*` refs. The CLI writes both `transcript.jsonl` and `transcript_hash.txt` to `/main` at condensation time. The API can optionally use it for cache invalidation or content-addressed lookups.
130	
131	### Integration with external agent protocol
132	
133	**New capability**: "compact_transcript" declared in the `info` response.
134	**New subcommand**: `compact-transcript`
135	**session-ref**: The `--session-ref` argument is the absolute file path to the agent's transcript file.
136	
137	`entire-agent-<name> compact-transcript --session-ref <path>`
138	
139	The plugin reads the raw transcript from disk, compacts it into Entire Transcript Format, and outputs JSON to stdout:
140	
141	```json
142	{
143	  "transcript": "<base64-encoded Entire Transcript Format JSONL>",
144	  "assets": [
145	    {"name": "img-001.png", "data": "<base64>", "media_type": "image/png"},
146	    {"name": "img-002.png", "data": "<base64>", "media_type": "image/jpg"}
147	  ]
148	}
149	```
150	
151	#### Output format
152	
153	- transcript (required): Base64-encoded Entire Transcript Format JSONL.
154	- assets (optional): Extracted binary data.
155	  - Each asset has a name, media_type, and base64-encoded `data`.
156	  
157	If the STDOUT size limit of 10 MB becomes an issue, we could consider implementing a chunked version similar to [`chunk-transcript`](https://docs.entire.io/cli/external-agents#chunk-transcript-max-size-%3Cn%3E).
158	  
159	#### Fallback behavior
160	
161	If the plugin doesn't declare `compact_transcript` capability, the CLI writes `full.jsonl` **only to `/full/current`** — nothing transcript-related is written to `/main` for that checkpoint (metadata and prompt are still written as usual). This means:
162	
163	- Old plugins continue working without changes
164	- New plugins opt into compaction when ready
165	- **No permanent `full.jsonl` on `/main`** — avoids leaving behind a large, never-compacted file on the permanent ref. If a plugin later adds compaction support, future checkpoints get compact transcripts on `/main` without stale `full.jsonl` files cluttering the append-only history.
166	- The CLI/API read path checks for `transcript.jsonl` on `/main` first, then falls back to `full.jsonl` on `/full/current`
167	  - This also helps develop the v2 format while working on the compaction mechanism in parallel
168	
169	**Why base64 encoding**: The `transcript` field contains UTF-8 JSONL bytes that the CLI writes byte-for-byte to `transcript.jsonl` on the `/main` ref. Base64 ensures byte-exact round-tripping — the plugin produces the final JSONL output and the CLI transports it without parsing or re-serialization. This avoids nested JSON escaping (JSONL lines contain quotes, backslashes, and potentially control characters from tool output that would all need escaping inside a JSON string) and is consistent with the encoding used by [`chunk-transcript`](https://docs.entire.io/cli/external-agents#chunk-transcript-max-size-%3Cn%3E). The `assets` array uses base64 for its `data` fields since those carry actual binary content (images, screenshots).
170	
171	### Git storage model: refs with generational rotation
172	
173	#### The problem with a single branch
174	
175	The current design stores all checkpoints in a single branch (`entire/checkpoints/v1`) under `refs/heads/`. Each `WriteCommitted` creates a new commit on top of the previous one, splicing a new checkpoint subtree into the root tree.
176	
177	Removing `full.jsonl` from the latest commit's tree does **not** reclaim space — every prior commit still references the old blob. The only way to free space on a single branch is to squash the entire history into one orphan commit and force-push — with all the downsides that entails (race conditions leading to data corruption, destroyed history, opaque GC timing, reconciliation complexity).
178	
179	#### Why refs instead of branches
180	
181	v2 stores everything under `refs/entire/` instead of `refs/heads/`. This is a deliberate choice:
182	
183	**Invisible in GitHub UI.** Branches (`refs/heads/*`) show up in the branch dropdown, the "compare & pull request" banner, and branch protection rules. Checkpoint refs are internal plumbing — they should not clutter the UI or prompt developers to open PRs against them. Custom ref namespaces under `refs/entire/` are invisible in the GitHub branch UI.
184	
185	**Refs can be pointed elsewhere without force-push.** A ref under `refs/entire/` can be updated to point to any commit — there's no fast-forward enforcement by default. This makes rotation trivial: point `current` to the new commit, point the old name to the archived commit. Branches under `refs/heads/` may have branch protection rules or require fast-forward pushes, adding friction.
186	
187	**No interference with branch-based workflows.** Branch count limits, CI triggers on branch push, branch cleanup bots, branch protection rules — none of these apply to custom refs. The checkpoint data lives in a parallel namespace that's invisible to standard git tooling unless explicitly accessed.
188	
189	**Clean fetch semantics.** The default refspec (`+refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/*`) only fetches branches. Refs under `refs/entire/` are never fetched unless the CLI explicitly requests them. This means `git clone` and `git fetch` never download checkpoint data by default — the CLI fetches exactly what it needs.
190	
191	**Consistent with v1 migration.** The current `entire/checkpoints/v1` lives under `refs/heads/` (it's a branch). Moving to `refs/entire/` in v2 creates a clean break — the CLI can detect which version is in use by checking the ref namespace.
192	
193	#### The solution: separate permanent and ephemeral data into different refs
194	
195	Three types of refs, each with different lifecycles:
196	
197	```
198	refs/entire/checkpoints/v2/main                ← permanent: metadata + compact transcripts
199	refs/entire/checkpoints/v2/full/current        ← active generation: raw logs (rotates when full)
200	refs/entire/checkpoints/v2/full/0000000000001  ← archived generation (deletable wholesale)
201	refs/entire/checkpoints/v2/full/0000000000002  ← archived generation (deletable wholesale)
202	```
203	
204	**`/main`** is a single append-only ref with linear commit history. Works like today's `entire/checkpoints/v1` but stores only small, permanent data: `metadata.json`, `transcript.jsonl`, `transcript_hash.txt`, `prompt.txt`, `assets/`. Never needs cleanup. Grows slowly. Standard merge logic for concurrent pushes (same as today — the existing `fetchAndMergeSessionsCommon` works here).
205	
206	**`/full/current`** is a ref that accumulates raw `full.jsonl` files as commits. Each checkpoint adds its raw logs to this ref's tree using the same sharded layout (`<id[:2]>/<id[2:]>/0/full.jsonl`). When it reaches a configured capacity (e.g., N checkpoints or M megabytes), it rotates:
207	
208	1. Rename `current` → next sequential number (e.g., `0000000000001`)
209	2. Create a fresh orphan `current`
210	
211	**`/full/NNNNNNNNNNNNN`** (archived generations) are frozen refs. Once all checkpoints in a generation age past the retention window, the entire ref is deleted — making the whole commit chain and all its raw log blobs unreachable in one operation.
212	
213	#### Why this works
214	
215	**Only 2-3 active refs at any time.** `/main` + `/full/current` + maybe one recent archived generation that hasn't been cleaned yet. Well within any hosting provider's limits, and invisible in the GitHub UI.
216	
217	**Cleanup = delete entire refs.** No tree surgery. No force-push. Just:
218	```bash
219	git push origin --delete refs/entire/checkpoints/v2/full/0000000000001
220	```
221	The entire commit chain becomes unreachable. Git GC reclaims all the large blobs. No need to understand the tree structure or modify individual files.
222	
223	**`/main` is never touched by cleanup.** It's append-only and permanent. The existing merge logic handles concurrent pushes. No new complexity here.
224	
225	**No force-push anywhere.** Deleting a ref is not a force-push — it's a ref deletion. The `/main` ref uses standard fast-forward pushes (with merge recovery, same as today). The `/full/current` ref also uses fast-forward pushes. When it rotates, the old ref is renamed and the new `current` starts as a fresh orphan.
226	
227	**Generation boundaries align with cleanup.** The generation size should be chosen so that a single generation spans roughly the retention window. Example: if retention is 14 days and a solo dev produces ~2 checkpoints/day, a generation of 30 checkpoints means each generation covers ~2 weeks. Cleanup can delete an entire generation once the newest checkpoint in it is past retention.
228	
229	#### Ref structure in detail
230	
231	```
232	refs/entire/checkpoints/v2/main → commit chain (linear history)
233	  HEAD tree:
234	    a3/b2c4d5e6f7/               # sharded by checkpoint ID (same as today)
235	      metadata.json               # CheckpointSummary
236	      0/
237	        metadata.json             # Session metadata
238	        transcript.jsonl          # Compact Entire Transcript Format
239	        transcript_hash.txt       # SHA-256 of transcript.jsonl
240	        prompt.txt
241	        assets/
242	          img-001.png
243	      1/
244	        metadata.json
245	        transcript.jsonl
246	        transcript_hash.txt
247	    f1/9e8d7c6b5a/
248	      ...
249	
250	refs/entire/checkpoints/v2/full/current → commit chain (linear history)
251	  HEAD tree:
252	    a3/b2c4d5e6f7/               # same shard structure
253	      0/
254	        full.jsonl                # Raw agent transcript for session 0
255	        content_hash.txt          # SHA-256 of full.jsonl
256	      1/
257	        full.jsonl                # Raw agent transcript for session 1
258	        content_hash.txt
259	    f1/9e8d7c6b5a/
260	      0/
261	        full.jsonl
262	        content_hash.txt
263	```
264	
265	The `/main` and `/full/current` trees use the same sharded path structure (`<id[:2]>/<id[2:]>/`). Given a checkpoint ID, the CLI/API knows exactly where to find data in both trees.
266	
267	#### Write path (CLI)
268	
269	At condensation time, the CLI writes to two refs:
270	
271	```go
272	// 1. Append metadata + compact transcript + transcript_hash to /main (same pattern as today)
273	mainTree := spliceCheckpointSubtree(mainRootTree, checkpointID, mainEntries)
274	mainCommit := createCommit(mainTree, mainParent, ...)
275	SetReference("refs/entire/checkpoints/v2/main", mainCommit)
276	
277	// 2. Append raw log + content_hash to /full/current
278	fullTree := spliceCheckpointSubtree(fullRootTree, checkpointID, fullEntries)
279	fullCommit := createCommit(fullTree, fullParent, ...)
280	SetReference("refs/entire/checkpoints/v2/full/current", fullCommit)
281	
282	// 3. Check if rotation is needed
283	if generationSize(fullTree) >= maxCheckpointsPerGeneration {
284	    rotate()  // rename current → next number, create fresh orphan current
285	}
286	```
287	
288	The write path is essentially the same as today's `WriteCommitted` — splice into a tree, create a commit on top. The only difference is writing to two refs instead of one, under `refs/entire/` instead of `refs/heads/`.
289	
290	#### Read path (CLI + API)
291	
292	**Read a specific checkpoint** (metadata + compact transcript):
293	```go
294	// Same as today — read from /main tree at HEAD
295	mainTree := getTree("entire/checkpoints/v2/main")
296	subtree := mainTree.Tree(checkpointID.Path())
297	// Read metadata.json, transcript.jsonl, etc.
298	```
299	
300	**Read raw transcript** (for `entire resume`):
301	```go
302	// Read from /full/current or search archived generations
303	fullTree := getTree("entire/checkpoints/v2/full/current")
304	subtree := fullTree.Tree(checkpointID.Path())
305	if subtree == nil {
306	    // Not in current generation — search archived generations
307	    for _, gen := range listArchivedGenerations() {
308	        genTree := getTree(gen)
309	        subtree = genTree.Tree(checkpointID.Path())
310	        if subtree != nil { break }
311	    }
312	}
313	// Read full.jsonl
314	```
315	
316	**List all checkpoints:** Same as today — walk the `/main` tree. Single tree, sharded directories, O(all checkpoints). No change.
317	
318	#### Push path
319	
320	Since refs under `refs/entire/` don't have remote-tracking refs by default, pushes use explicit refspecs. Custom refs also lack the "has unpushed" optimization available for branches (no remote-tracking ref to compare against), so the CLI always attempts the push and lets git handle the no-op case.
321	
322	All v2 refs are pushed to the same target as v1 checkpoints — either the user's push remote or the configured `checkpoint_remote`.
323	
324	```bash
325	# Push v2 refs (explicit refspecs since these aren't under refs/heads/)
326	git push origin refs/entire/checkpoints/v2/main:refs/entire/checkpoints/v2/main
327	git push origin refs/entire/checkpoints/v2/full/current:refs/entire/checkpoints/v2/full/current
328	git push origin refs/entire/checkpoints/v2/full/0000000000001:refs/entire/checkpoints/v2/full/0000000000001
329	
330	# Delete an archived generation
331	git push origin --delete refs/entire/checkpoints/v2/full/0000000000001
332	```
333	
334	The CLI enumerates all local refs matching `refs/entire/checkpoints/v2/full/*` and pushes each one alongside `/main`. This ensures archived generations reach the remote for cleanup and cross-machine `entire resume`.
335	
336	##### Merge recovery for `/main`
337	
338	`/main` contains only sharded checkpoint directories (`<id[:2]>/<id[2:]>/`) — no root-level files. Tree merges are always conflict-free: different checkpoint IDs land in different shard paths. The recovery pattern is the same as v1: fetch the remote ref, flatten both trees, combine entries, create a merge commit, push again.
339	
340	##### Merge recovery for `/full/current`
341	
342	`/full/current` also contains only sharded checkpoint directories during normal operation — `generation.json` is **not** written to `/full/current` (see "Generation rotation" below). This makes `/full/current` tree merges conflict-free, the same as `/main`.
343	
344	When a push of `/full/current` fails with non-fast-forward and no archived generations exist on the remote, the recovery is the same tree-merge as `/main`.
345	
346	##### Rotation conflict recovery
347	
348	When a push of `/full/current` fails and the remote has archived generations that don't exist locally, another machine has rotated `/full/current` since we last synced. In this case, the remote `/full/current` is a fresh orphan and our local `/full/current` shares a base with the latest archived generation.
349	
350	Instead of merging two divergent `/full/current` refs (which would duplicate checkpoint data across the archived generation and the merged result), the CLI merges the local `/full/current` **into the latest archived generation**:
351	
352	1. `git ls-remote` to discover remote archived generation refs
353	2. Fetch the latest archived generation (cheap — most blobs already local since we shared the same base)
354	3. Tree-merge local `/full/current` into the archived generation's tree
355	4. Git's content-addressing deduplicates automatically: shared checkpoint paths with identical blob hashes produce one entry
356	5. Update `generation.json` in the merged tree: the archive's existing `generation.json` survives the merge (local `/full/current` has no root-level files), but its `newest_checkpoint_at` may be stale. Read it, update `newest_checkpoint_at` if any merged checkpoint is newer, and write it back into the merged tree.
357	6. Push the updated archived generation (fast-forward from the archive's previous commit)
358	7. Fetch and adopt remote's `/full/current` as local
359	
360	This may cause the archived generation to slightly exceed the rotation threshold (e.g., 105 instead of 100), which is acceptable. The key property is preserved: **each checkpoint's raw transcript exists in exactly one generation**, so deleting a generation ref makes all its unique blobs unreachable for GC.
361	
362	**Example:**
363	
364	```
365	Starting state (synced): /full/current has 95 checkpoints
366	
367	User A: adds 7 → 102 → rotation triggers
368	  /full/0000000000001: 102 checkpoints (95 shared + 7 from A)
369	  /full/current: fresh orphan
370	  Pushed to remote.
371	
372	User B: adds 3 → 98 locally, pushes /full/current → non-fast-forward
373	  Recovery:
374	    1. ls-remote → discovers /full/0000000000001 (not local)
375	    2. Fetch /full/0000000000001
376	    3. Tree-merge local /full/current (98) into /full/0000000000001 (102)
377	       → 95 shared deduplicated, result: 105 unique checkpoints
378	    4. Update generation.json, push /full/0000000000001 → fast-forward
379	    5. Adopt remote /full/current as local
380	
381	Final state:
382	  /full/0000000000001: 105 checkpoints (no duplication)
383	  /full/current: fresh orphan
384	```
385	
386	#### Generation rotation
387	
388	The rotation threshold is checked by counting checkpoint shard directories in the `/full/current` tree — O(total checkpoints) in tree object reads, a few milliseconds at 100 checkpoints.
389	
390	`generation.json` is **only written at archive time** (when `/full/current` is rotated to a numbered ref), not on every write to `/full/current`. This ensures `/full/current` contains only sharded checkpoint directories, making tree merges during push recovery conflict-free.
391	
392	When `/full/current` reaches its capacity:
393	
394	```go
395	func rotate() {
396	    nextGen := nextGenerationNumber()  // e.g., "0000000000001"
397	
398	    // Write generation.json to the current tree before archiving
399	    gen := buildGenerationMetadata(currentTree)  // timestamps from tree walk
400	    currentTree = addGenerationJSON(currentTree, gen)
401	    currentCommit = createCommit(currentTree, currentParent, "Archive generation")
402	    SetReference("refs/entire/checkpoints/v2/full/current", currentCommit)
403	
404	    // Rename: current → numbered archive
405	    archiveRef := fmt.Sprintf("refs/entire/checkpoints/v2/full/%s", nextGen)
406	    SetReference(archiveRef, currentCommit)
407	
408	    // Create fresh orphan current (empty tree, no parent)
409	    emptyTree := buildEmptyTree()
410	    newCommit := createCommit(emptyTree, nil, "Start generation")
411	    SetReference("refs/entire/checkpoints/v2/full/current", newCommit)
412	}
413	```
414	
415	The generation number is zero-padded for lexicographic sorting. The next generation number is derived from existing archived ref names.
416	
417	#### Generation sizing
418	
419	The generation size controls the tradeoff between cleanup granularity and overhead:
420	
421	| Generation size | Cleanup granularity | Overhead |
422	|----------------|-------------------|----------|
423	| Small (10 checkpoints) | Fine — can delete soon after retention | More generations, more archived refs |
424	| Large (500 checkpoints) | Coarse — must wait for all 500 to age out | Fewer refs, but delays space reclamation |
425	
426	**Recommended default: ~100 checkpoints per generation.** For a solo dev doing ~2 checkpoints/day, this spans ~50 days — well past a 14-day retention window, so cleanup can delete a generation within weeks of its oldest checkpoint aging out. For a team of 5, a generation fills in ~10 days, giving even finer cleanup granularity.
427	
428	Generation metadata (`generation.json`) is written to the tree root at archive time only — not during normal writes to `/full/current`. This keeps `/full/current` free of root-level files, ensuring conflict-free tree merges during push recovery. The cleanup tool reads `generation.json` from archived generations to assess eligibility without walking the full tree.
429	
430	#### Cleanup path
431	
432	```
433	1. List archived generation refs: entire/checkpoints/v2/full/NNNNN...
434	2. For each generation, read generation.json → check newest_checkpoint_at
435	3. If newest checkpoint is older than RETENTION_DAYS:
436	   a. Optionally archive to cold storage
437	   b. Delete the ref: git push origin --delete entire/checkpoints/v2/full/0000000000001
438	4. Done — entire commit chain becomes unreachable, GC reclaims blobs
439	```
440	
441	No tree surgery. No force-push. No modifying `/main`. Just deleting self-contained archived refs.
442	
443	### Pinning: keeping raw logs forever
444	
445	Some sessions are worth preserving in full — critical debugging sessions, key architectural decisions, compliance-relevant work. Users need a way to exempt specific checkpoints from cleanup.
446	
447	#### How it works
448	
449	**Pin a checkpoint's raw log by copying it into `/main`.**
450	
451	The `/main` ref is already the permanent store. When a user pins a checkpoint, the CLI copies its `full.jsonl` from `/full/current` (or an archived generation) into the same checkpoint directory on `/main`, alongside `transcript.jsonl`:
452	
453	```
454	entire/checkpoints/v2/main → tree:
455	  a3/b2c4d5e6f7/
456	    metadata.json
457	    0/
458	      metadata.json
459	      transcript.jsonl       # compact format (always present on /main)
460	      transcript_hash.txt    # hash of transcript.jsonl (always present on /main)
461	      full.jsonl             # ← pinned: raw log copied here
462	      content_hash.txt       # ← pinned: copied alongside full.jsonl
463	      prompt.txt
464	      assets/
465	```
466	
467	Once pinned, the generation containing that checkpoint can be deleted normally — the raw log is safe in `/main`.
468	
469	#### CLI interface
470	
471	```bash
472	# Pin a checkpoint's raw logs (all sessions)
473	entire pin <checkpoint-id>
474	
475	# Pin with session filter
476	entire pin <checkpoint-id> --session 0
477	
478	# Unpin (remove full.jsonl from /main, if still available in a generation)
479	entire unpin <checkpoint-id>
480	
481	# List pinned checkpoints
482	entire session list --pinned
483	```
484	
485	The pin command:
486	1. Resolves the checkpoint ID
487	2. Finds `full.jsonl` and `content_hash.txt` in `/full/current` or an archived generation
488	3. Copies both blobs into the `/main` tree under the checkpoint's directory
489	4. Optionally marks the checkpoint as pinned in its `metadata.json` (adds `"pinned": true`)
490	
491	#### Read path for pinned logs
492	
493	The read path for `entire resume` naturally handles pinned logs — it already checks `/main` first:
494	
495	```go
496	// 1. Check /main (handles pinned logs)
497	mainTree := getTree("entire/checkpoints/v2/main")
498	subtree := mainTree.Tree(checkpointID.Path() + "/0")
499	if file, err := subtree.File("full.jsonl"); err == nil {
500	    return file  // Found pinned log in /main
501	}
502	
503	// 2. Check /full/current
504	// 3. Search archived generations
505	// (same as before)
506	```
507	
508	#### Why copy into `/main` instead of a separate `/full/keep` ref
509	
510	- **No extra refs.** A `/full/keep` ref is one more long-lived ref to push, fetch, and merge. Copying into `/main` adds zero refs.
511	- **Natural discovery.** The raw log lives right next to the compact transcript and metadata. No cross-ref lookups.
512	- **Cleanup stays simple.** The cleanup tool doesn't need to check a separate keep list or skip certain checkpoints within a generation. It just deletes generations unconditionally — pinned logs are already safe in `/main`.
513	- **Size is bounded.** Pinning is an explicit user action, not automatic. Users pin a handful of important sessions, not hundreds. The size impact on `/main` is controlled by user intent.
514	
515	#### Retaining all raw logs (compliance mode)
516	
517	For teams that need full audit trails, a setting disables generation cleanup:
518	
519	```json
520	{
521	  "strategy_options": {
522	    "retain_raw_logs": true
523	  }
524	}
525	```
526	
527	This keeps all `/full/*` generations indefinitely — the cleanup tool skips deletion. The generational structure still provides bounded ref sizes and clean rotation. If the team later decides to start cleaning up, they just remove the setting and old generations become eligible for deletion — no migration needed.
528	
529	This pairs well with `checkpoint_remote` to keep the storage impact out of the code repository.
530	
531	### Interaction with checkpoint remote
532	
533	When `checkpoint_remote` is configured (checkpoints pushed to a separate repository), all `refs/entire/checkpoints/v2/*` refs are pushed there. The cleanup tool targets that repository for generation deletion. The cleanup tool reuses the same settings (`strategy_options.checkpoint_remote`) and protocol detection logic as the CLI's `PrePush`.
534	
535	### Cold storage archive (optional)
536	
537	Before deleting an archived generation, the cleanup tool can optionally upload its raw transcripts to cold storage (S3 Glacier, GCS Archive, etc.). The checkpoint metadata in `/main` could store an `archive_ref` for retrieval if ever needed. This preserves full fidelity for forensics or debugging without bloating the git repository.
538	
539	## Migration
540	
541	### From v1 (branch) to v2 (refs)
542	
543	Existing repos have all data on the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch (under `refs/heads/`). Migration path:
544	
545	1. **CLI reads from both v1 and v2.** On read, check v2 `/main` ref first, fall back to v1 branch. This allows a gradual transition.
546	2. **New writes go to v2.** After upgrade, condensation writes metadata to `/main` and raw logs to `/full/current` under `refs/entire/`. The v1 branch stops growing.
547	3. **Migration tool converts v1 → v2.** Reads the v1 tree, splits each checkpoint: metadata+compact transcript → `/main`, raw logs → `/full/current` (or directly into a numbered generation). Then deletes the v1 branch.
548	4. **Backfill `transcript.jsonl` for old checkpoints.** The migration tool generates compact transcripts from `full.jsonl` using agent-specific parsing (same logic the CLI already has). Since the tool is independently deployable, parsing rules can be updated and re-run.
549	
550	The v1 branch and v2 refs can coexist during the transition period.
551	
552	## Alternatives Considered
553	
554	**Post-hoc stripping only (original RFD).** Requires the cleanup tool to understand every agent's transcript format and apply the correct stripping rules. Version skew between CLI and cleanup tool could produce inconsistent results. Dual-write eliminates this because the CLI writes the compact format at recording time.
555	
556	**Compact in the CLI at condensation time (strip in place).** Two users condensing simultaneously would both try to compact old checkpoints. Since stripping logic may differ across CLI versions, this produces divergent blobs and push conflicts. Rejected.
557	
558	**Separate compacted branch.** Write compacted data to a second branch (e.g., `entire/checkpoints/v2-compacted`), keep `v1` append-only. Doubles branch count, adds read-path complexity in the API (check compacted branch first, fall back to v1). Rejected.
559	
560	**One branch per user for raw transcripts (Georg's suggestion).** Store raw transcripts on per-user branches for easy pruning without conflicts. Interesting but adds complexity: branch proliferation, discovery logic, and the CLI would need to know the user identity to pick the right branch. The generational `/full/*` refs achieve the same conflict-free cleanup without per-user branches.
561	
562	**One ref per checkpoint (split refs).** Each checkpoint gets its own ref(s) — `/main` for metadata, `/N/full` for raw logs. Cleanup is elegant (just delete refs), but ref count grows linearly with checkpoint count: 1,000 checkpoints = 2,000+ refs. GitHub recommends staying under 5,000 branches, and every ref is advertised during fetch negotiation. Teams with months of history would hit this limit. Rejected in favor of generational approach that caps refs at ~3.
563	
564	**Single ref per checkpoint (no split).** Same ref count problem as above, plus cleanup requires tree surgery instead of ref deletion. Rejected.
565	
566	**Single branch with squash cleanup.** Keep the current `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch. Cleanup squashes entire history into one orphan commit and force-pushes. Works but requires force-push (races with concurrent CLI pushes), destroys history, and depends on opaque server-side GC. Rejected in favor of generational approach.
567	
568	**Server-side compaction in the API.** The API already reads transcripts — it could compact on read. But the API shouldn't write to user repositories, and this couples compaction to API deployment. Rejected.
569	
570	## Domains Touched
571	
572	- **CLI** — dual-write to `/main` (metadata + compact transcript + assets) and `/full/current` (raw logs) under `refs/entire/`; generation rotation; pin support
573	- **API** — read `transcript.jsonl` from `/main` ref; fall back to `full.jsonl` on `/full/current` for plugins without compaction support; fall back to `full.jsonl` on v1 branch during migration
574	- **Cleanup tool** — new standalone tool (shipped as GitHub Action + CLI command); deletes archived `/full/*` generation refs
575	- **Infrastructure** — cold storage bucket if archive is enabled (optional)
576	
577	## Success Signal
578	
579	- `/main` ref grows slowly (metadata + compact transcripts only, ~96% smaller than today)
580	- `/full/current` rotates at bounded size — no single ref grows unbounded
581	- After cleanup deletes archived generations, all raw log blobs become unreachable
582	- `entire resume` continues to work for sessions within the retention window
583	- API reads `transcript.jsonl` for all new checkpoints without agent-specific parsing
584	- No force-push required — cleanup is ref deletion, writes are fast-forward
585	- Only 2-3 active refs at any time — well within hosting provider limits
586	- Existing merge logic for concurrent pushes works unchanged on `/main`
587	- No data loss — `/main` is never modified by cleanup
588	
589	## Prototype
590	
591	[20260226-transcript-compaction](https://github.com/entirehq/ephemera/tree/main/tasks/20260226-transcript-compaction) in ephemera — Python script implementing the stripping logic with batch analysis mode.
592	
593	Results from the prototype across 10 transcripts:
594	
595	```
596	Original:  158.34 MB
597	Stripped:    5.51 MB  (96.5% reduction)
598	```
599	
600	## Open Questions
601	
602	1. **Sharing parsing logic** — The CLI (Go) and cleanup tool write the compact format. The API reads it. How do we keep the format definition shared? A JSON Schema or protobuf definition?
603	2. ~~**Content hash** — Should `content_hash.txt` hash the raw transcript or the compact one (or both)?~~ **Resolved:** Both. `content_hash.txt` hashes the raw transcript and lives on `/full/*` alongside `full.jsonl`. `transcript_hash.txt` hashes the compact transcript and lives on `/main` alongside `transcript.jsonl`. See "Content hash placement" section.
604	3. **Cleanup tool language** — Should it be Go (share code with CLI), or a standalone script (easier to update independently)?
605	4. **Generation sizing** — What's the right default? Checkpoint count vs total size? Should it be configurable per-repo or fixed?
606	5. ~~**Generation metadata** — Where to store `generation.json` (tree root of each generation)? What fields: checkpoint count, oldest/newest timestamps, total size?~~ **Resolved:** `generation.json` is written to the tree root at archive time only (not during writes to `/full/current`). Fields: `oldest_checkpoint_at`, `newest_checkpoint_at` (timestamps only — no checkpoint list, since the tree structure itself is the authoritative source for checkpoint membership). Keeping `/full/current` free of root-level files ensures conflict-free tree merges during push recovery. See "Generation rotation" and "Push path" sections.
607	6. ~~**Concurrent rotation** — If two CLI instances both detect that `/full/current` is at capacity, both try to rotate. The rename is atomic (ref update), but we need to handle the race.~~ **Resolved:** Re-read `/full/current` before rotating. If it's below the threshold, another instance already rotated — skip. On push, the rotation conflict recovery merges local data into the latest archived generation. See "Rotation conflict recovery" in the push path section.
608	7. **Resume across generations** — `entire resume` needs to find the raw log for a specific checkpoint. If it's in an archived generation, the CLI needs to search multiple refs. Should `/main` metadata include a pointer to which generation holds each checkpoint's raw log?
609	8. **v1 → v2 migration** — How aggressive should migration be? Auto-migrate on first write? Explicit `entire migrate` command? Background migration?
610	9. **Pin UX** — Should pinning prompt for confirmation (since it copies potentially large data into `/main`)? Should `entire session list` show pin status? Should there be a size warning?

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write comprehensive implementation plans assuming the engineer has zero context for our codebase and questionable taste. Document everything they need to know: which files to touch for each task, code, testing, docs they might need to check, how to test it. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

Assume they are a skilled developer, but know almost nothing about our toolset or problem domain. Assume they don't know good test design very well.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** This should be run in a dedicated worktree (created by brainstorming skill).

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Bite-Sized Task Granularity

**Each step is one action (2-5 minutes):**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Write minimal implementation**

```python
def function(input):
    return expected
```

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## No Placeholders

Every step must contain the actual content an engineer needs. These are **plan failures** — never write them:
- "TBD", "TODO", "implement later", "fill in details"
- "Add appropriate error handling" / "add validation" / "handle edge cases"
- "Write tests for the above" (without actual test code)
- "Similar to Task N" (repeat the code — the engineer may be reading tasks out of order)
- Steps that describe what to do without showing how (code blocks required for code steps)
- References to types, functions, or methods not defined in any task

## Remember
- Exact file paths always
- Complete code in every step — if a step changes code, show the code
- Exact commands with expected output
- DRY, YAGNI, TDD, frequent commits

## Self-Review

After writing the complete plan, look at the spec with fresh eyes and check the plan against it. This is a checklist you run yourself — not a subagent dispatch.

**1. Spec coverage:** Skim each section/requirement in the spec. Can you point to a task that implements it? List any gaps.

**2. Placeholder scan:** Search your plan for red flags — any of the patterns from the "No Placeholders" section above. Fix them.

**3. Type consistency:** Do the types, method signatures, and property names you used in later tasks match what you defined in earlier tasks? A function called `clearLayers()` in Task 3 but `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug.

If you find issues, fix them inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on. If you find a spec requirement with no task, add the task.

## Execution Handoff

After saving the plan, offer execution choice:

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Two execution options:**

**1. Subagent-Driven (recommended)** - I dispatch a fresh subagent per task, review between tasks, fast iteration

**2. Inline Execution** - Execute tasks in this session using executing-plans, batch execution with checkpoints

**Which approach?"**

**If Subagent-Driven chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development
- Fresh subagent per task + two-stage review

**If Inline Execution chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:executing-plans
- Batch execution with checkpoints for review

// compactTranscriptForV2 produces the Entire Transcript Format (transcript.jsonl)
// from a raw agent transcript. Returns nil if compaction cannot be performed
// (nil agent, empty transcript, or compaction error) — callers treat nil as
// "skip writing transcript.jsonl to /main".
func compactTranscriptForV2(ctx context.Context, ag agent.Agent, transcript []byte, checkpointTranscriptStart int) []byte {
	if ag == nil || len(transcript) == 0 {
		return nil
	}
	if !settings.IsCheckpointsV2Enabled(ctx) {
		return nil
	}

	compacted, err := compact.Compact(transcript, compact.MetadataFields{
		Agent:      string(ag.Name()),
		CLIVersion: versioninfo.Version,
		StartLine:  checkpointTranscriptStart,
	})
	if err != nil {

			slog.String("agent", string(ag.Name())),
			slog.String("error", err.Error()),
		)
		return nil
	}
	return compacted
}

## Design Decisions

1. **Compaction in the strategy layer, not the checkpoint layer.** The checkpoint layer writes bytes it receives. The strategy layer has the agent context and CLI version needed for `compact.MetadataFields`. This follows the existing pattern where redaction happens in the checkpoint layer but data preparation happens in the strategy layer.

2. **`CompactTranscript` as an optional field on options structs.** When nil, `writeMainSessionToSubdirectory` skips writing `transcript.jsonl` — metadata and prompts are still written. This implements the RFD's fallback behavior: "If the plugin doesn't declare `compact_transcript` capability, the CLI writes `full.jsonl` only to `/full/current` — nothing transcript-related is written to `/main`."

3. **Using the built-in `compact` package, not the external agent protocol.** The `compact-transcript` subcommand for external agents (described in the RFD) does not exist yet. The built-in `compact` package already handles Claude Code (JSONL), Gemini (JSON), and OpenCode formats. External agent compaction can be added as a separate task.

4. **No chunking for compact transcripts.** The compact format is ~96.5% smaller than raw transcripts. A 46 MB raw transcript compresses to ~40 KB. Chunking is unnecessary for the compact format at these sizes.

5. **`transcript_hash.txt` on `/main`, `content_hash.txt` on `/full/current`.** Per RFD-009: each hash file lives alongside the data it validates. The compact transcript hash lives on `/main`; the raw transcript hash lives on `/full/current`.

**DONE_WITH_CONCERNS:** The implementer completed the work but flagged doubts. Read the concerns before proceeding. If the concerns are about correctness or scope, address them before review. If they're observations (e.g., "this file is getting large"), note them and proceed to review.

**NEEDS_CONTEXT:** The implementer needs information that wasn't provided. Provide the missing context and re-dispatch.

**BLOCKED:** The implementer cannot complete the task. Assess the blocker:
1. If it's a context problem, provide more context and re-dispatch with the same model
2. If the task requires more reasoning, re-dispatch with a more capable model
3. If the task is too large, break it into smaller pieces
4. If the plan itself is wrong, escalate to the human

**Never** ignore an escalation or force the same model to retry without changes. If the implementer said it's stuck, something needs to change.

## Advantages

**vs. Manual execution:**
- Subagents follow TDD naturally
- Fresh context per task (no confusion)
- Parallel-safe (subagents don't interfere)
- Subagent can ask questions (before AND during work)

**vs. Executing Plans:**
- Same session (no handoff)
- Continuous progress (no waiting)
- Review checkpoints automatic

**Efficiency gains:**
- No file reading overhead (controller provides full text)
- Controller curates exactly what context is needed
- Subagent gets complete information upfront
- Questions surfaced before work begins (not after)

**Quality gates:**
- Self-review catches issues before handoff
- Two-stage review: spec compliance, then code quality
- Review loops ensure fixes actually work
- Spec compliance prevents over/under-building
- Code quality ensures implementation is well-built

**Cost:**
- More subagent invocations (implementer + 2 reviewers per task)
- Controller does more prep work (extracting all tasks upfront)
- Review loops add iterations
- But catches issues early (cheaper than debugging later)

## Red Flags

**Never:**
- Start implementation on main/master branch without explicit user consent
- Skip reviews (spec compliance OR code quality)
- Proceed with unfixed issues
- Dispatch multiple implementation subagents in parallel (conflicts)
- Make subagent read plan file (provide full text instead)
- Skip scene-setting context (subagent needs to understand where task fits)
- Ignore subagent questions (answer before letting them proceed)
- Accept "close enough" on spec compliance (spec reviewer found issues = not done)
- Skip review loops (reviewer found issues = implementer fixes = review again)
- Let implementer self-review replace actual review (both are needed)
- **Start code quality review before spec compliance is ✅** (wrong order)
- Move to next task while either review has open issues

**If subagent asks questions:**
- Answer clearly and completely
- Provide additional context if needed
- Don't rush them into implementation

**If reviewer finds issues:**
- Implementer (same subagent) fixes them
- Reviewer reviews again
- Repeat until approved
- Don't skip the re-review

**If subagent fails task:**
- Dispatch fix subagent with specific instructions
- Don't try to fix manually (context pollution)

5. **Condensation wiring** — compact transcript generated at post-commit condensation time
